body:
Three readings are now on the table: the account's ambiguity/specification reading; the objection's renegotiation and legitimacy readings; and the rival's unit-versus-privacy axis. My first move is to stop treating these as competitors that one test can sort out. They are not exclusive, and in a real flat they probably coexist — an agreement can be vague about "by when," and also be resented as a binding, and also be disputed by someone who thinks a flat shouldn't generate bindings at all. The useful question is not which reading is true, but which is load-bearing right now.

What I accept. The objection is right that the account's reframing does more work than the material carries: the reported pattern — agreement now, disagreement later about what it meant — is consistent with all three readings, and the account's own o1 names this before proceeding as if ambiguity had won. I would keep the ambiguity reading as one hypothesis, no longer the default front-runner. The objection is also right about the test: falling recurrence on specified items does not discriminate. But the same criticism applies to the rival's test. Pulling back from a written arrangement does not uniquely indicate a privacy reading; someone can pull back because the document feels infantilizing, because they read it as an escalation, or because they are conflict-avoidant generally. Both tests are weak signals, not verdicts. They are worth using as accumulating observations, not as one-shot discriminators. The rival's second axis is genuinely additive — it names a question the account's plan assumes away — and the rival's truce-shaped arrangements (owned zones, default-outcome rotations) are, to my eye, the most robust single move in the whole set, because they are the only proposal that does not require the household to settle the meaning question first. They reduce ambiguity (account), reduce the renegotiation surface (objection), and reduce mutual exposure (rival). That robustness across readings is a reason to try them early, not last.

What I would revise or downweight. The rival's opening move — ask each flatmate what the flat is — is the heaviest question in the toolkit, and in one-to-one form it is still a big ask. The account warned that "we need to talk about the house" invites the same argument; "what kind of household is this?" is larger. I would not lead with it. The rival's r10 mitigates this by keeping the conversations separate, but understates the risk. I would let the unit/privacy question emerge from something concrete — a proposal about zones, or a reaction to a small written note — rather than pose it as the framing question. The account's three-column spec (done / by when / fallback) is still worth trying, but as one probe among several, not as the plan; the objection's sequencing point stands.

What I would foreground. Order matters less than the form of the first move. All three drafts converge on: low-stakes, one-to-one, concrete, no household-wide summit, no moral language about effort. That convergence is the strongest practical thing in the material. Start there, with one item and one person, and treat the content as secondary to whether the contact itself goes better. Then the robust move: propose an arrangement that minimizes what anyone has to agree on — a zone you own, or a rotation with a default outcome nobody has to negotiate in the moment — and present it as a truce, not a settlement. That is the move I would try before deciding which reading is right, precisely because it does not require deciding.

What I would leave open. Whether the avoidance is about the flat at all. None of the three drafts considers that the withdrawing friend may be dealing with something outside the household — workload, health, an unrelated conflict — which would make the whole frame a misdiagnosis. The material does not say, so it stays open. Whether the withdrawing friend is acting reasonably stays open too; the rival's r9 flags this and I agree. And whether the disagreements are about meaning, about binding, or about what a flat is, the material does not settle; I would be suspicious of any plan that claims it does.

Working synthesis, held at conjecture: the form of the conversation and the question of what the household is are more likely to be load-bearing than the crispness of the chore terms. The cheapest way to test that is to change the form first and watch whether the avoidance eases.
